ceramic.snippet:
Visible light photoredox catalysis has enabled easy access to acyl radicals under mild reaction conditions. Reactive acyl radicals, generated from various acyl precursors such as aldehydes, α-ketoacids, carboxylic acids, anhydrides, acyl thioesters, acyl chlorides, or acyl silanes, can undergo a diverse range of synthetically useful transformations, which were previously difficult or inaccessible.

 Over the past decade, various research groups reported the visible light mediated generation of acyl radicals using photoredox catalysts, metallaphotocatalysts, hypervalent iodine photocatalysts, or organic photocatalysts. This review aims to provide an overview of recent progress in such visible-light driven acyl radical generation using aldehydes, α-ketocarboxylic acids, carboxylic acids, carboxylic acid anhydrides, acyl thioesters, acid chlorides, or acylsilanes as acyl radical precursors ( Scheme 2 ). The scope, limitations, and the proposed reaction mechanism of each transformation are discussed. It is noteworthy that most of the reactions described in this review proceed through photoredox catalytic cycles, but the radical chain mechanism cannot be excluded.

 Simple and inexpensive carboxylic acids can be an alternate source from which to generate the acyl radical by visible light photoredox catalysis (PC). Base-mediated photocatalytic oxidation, decarboxylation and further carbonylation of the  in-situ generated alkyl radical by carbon monoxide (CO) can afford acyl radicals. Alternatively, the carboxylic acid is converted to its redox-active ester by the use of an activating agent (X = active electrophile) which can be reduced by photoredox catalyst (PC) to form the acyl radical ( Scheme 55 ). deepseek.snippet:
**Anhydride Synthesis:** As the name implies, an anhydride is the product when two carboxylic acids join by "losing" a water molecule. This is accomplished by heating a pure sample of the acid, until the water is driven off. For example:

\[\text{CH}_3\text{C}-\text{OH}+\text{HO}-\text{C}\text{CH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} \text{CH}_3\text{C}-\text{O}-\text{C}\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\]

This reaction is reversible; all that needs to be done is that the anhydride is heated with water.

The name of the anhydride is based on the carboxylic acid (or acids) that are used in its synthesis. The name is basically the name of the acid where "acid" is replaced by "anhydride". So, for example, the molecule above would be "acetic anhydride".

The usefulness of these two derivatives lies mainly in their use as synthetic reagents for amides and esters.

## Introduction

The hydrolysis of acid anhydrides with water represents a cornerstone reaction in organic chemistry, transforming these highly reactive compounds into their corresponding carboxylic acids. In this process, an acid anhydride, characterized by the (RCO)2O structure where two acyl groups are linked by an oxygen bridge, reacts with a single molecule of water to yield two molecules of carboxylic acid (2 RCOOH) for acyclic variants. This reaction exemplifies nucleophilic acyl substitution, underscoring the exceptional electrophilicity of the anhydride's carbonyl carbons due to the stabilizing effect of the adjacent carbonyl group. Its significance extends beyond fundamental reactivity; it plays a pivotal role in synthetic methodologies, industrial processes like aspirin production, and biochemical pathways where anhydrides serve as activated forms of acids.

Historically and practically, anhydride hydrolysis highlights the balance between reactivity and control in organic synthesis. Unlike less reactive esters or amides, anhydrides undergo hydrolysis rapidly at ambient conditions without catalysts, driven by the formation of a proficient carboxylate leaving group. This efficiency makes it indispensable for preparing carboxylic acids from anhydrides, which are often more stable storage forms. Environmentally, understanding this reaction aids in assessing the fate of anhydride pollutants in aqueous systems, while in academia, it serves as a model for teaching mechanistic organic chemistry. Key themes include the relief of strain in cyclic anhydrides, such as maleic or succinic, which hydrolyze even more readily, producing diacids like phthalic acid from phthalic anhydride. Overall, this reaction bridges theoretical principles with real-world applications, influencing pharmaceuticals, polymers, and materials science.

#### Learn More  
Carboxylic acid anhydrides conceptually derive from the condensation reaction of two carboxylic acid molecules, where a water molecule is eliminated from the hydroxyl of one acid and the hydrogen of the other, forging the oxygen bridge between acyl moieties. This dehydration process is thermodynamically challenging due to the stability of water and carboxylic acids, often requiring catalysts or dehydrating agents to shift equilibrium toward anhydride formation. Understanding this origin highlights why anhydrides serve as activated acyl transfer agents, more reactive than parent acids because the anhydride linkage weakens upon nucleophilic attack, enabling applications in acylation reactions across pharmaceuticals and materials science.

What is a nonsymmetric anhydride in organic chemistry?  
Anhydride Derived From Two Different Carboxylic Acids
Carboxylic Acid Derivative  
#### Learn More  
As carboxylic acid derivatives, nonsymmetric anhydrides occupy a pivotal position in the reactivity series, where their labile nature arises from the anhydride oxygen's ability to bridge two acyl groups, enabling efficient nucleophilic acyl substitution. This classification explains their superior reactivity over esters and amides due to the resonance-stabilized carboxylate leaving group, which departs more readily than alkoxide or amide ions. Their significance lies in transforming less reactive carboxylic acids into potent acylating agents, essential for multistep syntheses in pharmaceuticals and natural product chemistry.  
What is the etymology of nonsymmetric anhydride?  
Refers To Anhydride Without Water From Mixed Acids  
#### Learn More  
The etymology 'nonsymmetric anhydride' derives from 'anhydride,' meaning 'without water,' referring to the removal of H2O from two carboxylic acid molecules, combined with 'nonsymmetric' to denote the incorporation of dissimilar acid residues. This naming convention illuminates the mechanistic foundation: symmetric anhydrides like acetic anhydride ((CH3CO)2O) form homogeneously, while nonsymmetric variants introduce heterogeneity for targeted reactivity. Grasping this terminology aids in comprehending their evolution from simple dehydrating agents to sophisticated tools in asymmetric synthesis, emphasizing structural diversity's impact on function.

The nomenclature of acid halides starts with the name of the corresponding carboxylic acid. The –ic acid ending is removed and replaced with the ending -yl followed by the name of the halogen with an –ide ending. This is true for both common and IUPAC nomenclature. The carbonyl carbon is given the #1 location number. It is not necessary to include the location number in the name because it is assumed that the functional group will be on the end of the parent chain.

Nomenclature of Anhydrides

The acid anhydride functional group results when two carboxylic acids combine and lose water (anhydride = without water). Symmetrical acid anhydrides are named like carboxylic acids except the ending -acid is replaced with -anhydride . This is true for both the IUPAC and Common nomenclature.

Acetic anhydride is often used to prepare acetate esters from alcohols.

seltz.title: Anhydrides: Formation and Acylating Power — Organic Chemistry
seltz.snippet: Picture a chemist trying to acetylate an amine buried inside a fragile, polyfunctional natural product. This substrate would fall apart in the presence of the HCl liberated by acetyl chloride. The classic fix is acetic anhydride. It is a milder acylating agent, buffered by its own acetate leaving group. It reacts cleanly with the amine and leaves behind acetic acid rather than a strong mineral acid. This single design choice — trading a chloride leaving group for a carboxylate leaving group — is the entire story of anhydride reactivity. It is worth understanding at the level of orbitals and arrows rather than as a memorized fact. Anhydrides sit one rung below acid chlorides on The Reactivity Ladder of Acyl Derivatives. They earn that position for a precise electronic reason. The leaving group of an anhydride is a carboxylate, a far better-stabilized anion. It is more easily expelled, but less activating, than the chloride ion that departs from an acid chloride — wait, chloride is in fact an excellent leaving group. The true comparison is subtler, and it is exactly what this article dissects. The key is that a carboxylate oxygen lone pair can donate into the adjacent carbonyl of an anhydride. It does this just as effectively as an alkoxide-type oxygen would. So anhydrides are both moderately electrophilic *and* moderately good leaving groups. This compromise makes them the acylating agent of choice whenever a chloride's excess reactivity, or its corrosive HCl byproduct, would be a liability. This article builds anhydride chemistry from the ground up. It covers how symmetrical and mixed anhydrides are synthesized: from acid chlorides, from acid-catalyzed dehydration, and via mixed-anhydride strategies used in peptide coupling. It also covers how they react as nucleophilic acyl substitution partners with alcohols, amines, and water. Every step is drawn out with curved arrows on a tetrahedral intermediate.

seltz.title: The Peptide Bond and Its Formation — Biochemistry · Fermi
seltz.snippet: Every protein in your body — hemoglobin ferrying oxygen, actin pulling your muscles taut, the antibodies patrolling your bloodstream — is built from the same simple chemical joint. It is repeated hundreds or thousands of times. That joint is the peptide bond. It is the amide linkage formed when the carboxyl group of one amino acid condenses with the amino group of another. It looks trivial on paper — lose a water molecule, draw a new C–N bond. Yet this single reaction, run with exquisite control by the ribosome, is the entire basis of the polymer chemistry of life. Understanding *how* this bond forms — mechanistically, energetically, and stereochemically — matters far beyond satisfying curiosity about biochemical bookkeeping. The peptide bond's formation is thermodynamically uphill in water. This is precisely why cells must couple it to ATP hydrolysis. It is also why laboratory peptide synthesis requires activating reagents. Its planarity and partial double-bond character, previewed here and treated in full elsewhere, dictate the entire secondary-structure repertoire of proteins. The α-helix and β-sheet exist only because rotation around this bond is restricted. Every drug that targets a protease traces back to this chemistry. Every question about why proteins fold the way they do does too. So does every attempt to synthesize a peptide therapeutic. The big picture is this: amino acids are difunctional monomers. Each carries a nucleophile (the α-amino group) and an electrophile precursor (the carboxyl group). Direct combination of a free amine and a free carboxylic acid does not spontaneously churn out amide bonds at useful rates. The carboxylate is a poor electrophile. The reaction is also entropically and enthalpically unfavorable in aqueous solution. Nature's solution, executed on the ribosome, is to first "activate" the carbonyl carbon. This is done by esterifying it to a high-energy intermediate

# Conversion to Acid Anhydride

## Introduction to Carboxylic Acid Anhydrides

Carboxylic acid anhydrides are very unstable derivatives of carboxylic acids. They are strongly electrophilic and react with even the weakest nucleophiles. For example, acetic anhydride reacts readily with water forming acetic acid.

Anhydrides are important reagents to transfer acyl substituents to O and N atoms in various molecules. For example, the synthesis of aspirin involves the acetylation of salicylic acid. [...] ### Synthesis of Acid Anhydrides

Since acid anhydrides are very unstable, there aren’t many synthetic approaches to prepare them. We’ll discuss a couple here.

### Dehydration of Carboxylic Acids

Acetic anhydride can be prepared by heating acetic acid at 800 °C.

Dicarboxylic acids on the other hand react under very mild conditions and form cyclic anhydrides. The following reaction shows the formation of succinic anhydride from succinic acid. [...] ### The reaction of Acyl Halides with Carboxylate Salts

This is the most straightforward method for the synthesis of an acid anhydride and gives a good yield of products. The following reaction shows the reaction of acetyl chloride with sodium acetate to give acetic anhydride.

The reaction mechanism is quite simple. It starts with the nucleophilic attack of acetate ion on the acetyl halide molecule to form a tetrahedral intermediate which collapses to yield acetic anhydride.

## Hydrolysis of the anhydride product

An acid anhydride reacts with water to give carboxylic acids. One molecule of ethanoic anhydride gives two molecules of ethanoic acid: (CH3CO)2O + H2O → 2 CH3CO2H. [...] Water adds to an acyl carbon, and proton transfers and collapse of the tetrahedral intermediate split the acyl–oxygen bond. A mixed anhydride gives the two corresponding acids; in basic solution, carboxylate salts are the appropriate endpoints. This reaction explains the product's moisture sensitivity. It is not simply the reverse of the acid-chloride/carboxylate preparation, because hydrolysis uses a different nucleophile.

## Practical Tips & Pitfalls [...] | Key pivot | The nucleophile is the carboxylate oxygen, not the neutral acid. Mixed anhydride retains the original carbonyl and adds an acetyl fragment. |
| When it fails | Water during step 2 hydrolyzes CH₃COCl; trace base must be consumed before acylation so the acid chloride survives long enough to react. |

Organic anhydrides tend to follow a nucleophilic acyl substitution path — water attacks the carbonyl carbon, kicks out the carboxylate, and boom: two acid molecules. Simple on paper. That’s two acetic acid molecules forming per anhydride unit. 

Water’s oxygen, rich in electrons, dives at the electrophilic carbon of the carbonyl group in the anhydride. This isn’t a polite handshake — it’s a collision with purpose. A tetrahedral intermediate forms, unstable, with a negative charge on one oxygen and a positive charge on the other. But because the adjacent group is another carbonyl — electron-withdrawing — it stabilizes the negative charge just enough to let the bond break. Then the acetate ion peels away, taking electrons with it, leaving behind protonated acetic acid. Which immediately deprotonates. And just like that, you’ve got your products.
